kcet|Chemistry|2005|31||0|0:
Three clues, and together they fix the compound.
It **reduces Fehling's solution**, so it contains an aldehyde group.
On **oxidation it gives a monocarboxylic acid**, confirming a single –CHO.
It is made by the **action of chlorine on ethyl alcohol**, which chlorinates the methyl group
and oxidises the alcohol:
C₂H₅OH + 4Cl₂ ⇒ CCl₃CHO + 5HCl
That product is **chloral**, trichloroethanal, CCl₃CHO — which matches the formula C₂Cl₃OH
as written ✓
On oxidation it gives trichloroacetic acid, CCl₃COOH, a monocarboxylic acid ✓
Chloroform (1) has no aldehyde group and will not reduce Fehling's; methyl chloride (3) has
only one carbon; monochloroacetic acid (4) is already the acid, not the aldehyde.
Chloral with water gives chloral hydrate, the first synthetic sedative.
∴ chloral.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|32||0|0.s:
Reactivity in nucleophilic substitution depends on two things: the halogen and the class of
carbon.
**The halogen** — the C–X bond must break, so the weaker the bond the faster the reaction.
C–Br (285 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than C–Cl (327), and Br⁻ is also the better leaving group,
being the larger and more stable anion. So bromides beat chlorides.
**The carbon** — a secondary halide ionises more readily than a primary one, because the
secondary carbocation formed in SN1 is stabilised by two alkyl groups rather than one.
So 2-position beats 1-position.
Putting both together, the most reactive is the one that is secondary **and** a bromide:
2-bromopropane ✓
The order runs 2-bromopropane > 1-bromopropane > 2-chloropropane > 1-chloropropane.
∴ 2-bromopropane.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|33||0|0:
Look for the reaction an alcohol gives but a phenol does not.
(1) Both esterify with a carboxylic acid, though phenol needs the more reactive acid chloride
or anhydride — so this does not cleanly separate them.
(4) Both liberate hydrogen with sodium, giving the alkoxide or the phenoxide. Phenol, being
the stronger acid, reacts even more readily.
(2) Neither reacts with ammonia under ordinary conditions.
(3) The **iodoform test** distinguishes them. It requires a CH₃–CH(OH)– group, which ethanol
has, so ethanol with I₂/NaOH gives the yellow crystals of CHI₃:
C₂H₅OH + 4I₂ + 6NaOH ⇒ CHI₃↓ + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H₂O
Phenol has its –OH on an aromatic ring with no adjacent CH₃ at all, so no iodoform can form.
(Phenol does react with I₂/NaOH, but by substitution on the ring, not by the iodoform route.)
∴ it forms yellow crystals of iodoform.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|34||0|0.s:
Take the clues one at a time.
**Boiling point 78 °C** with a pleasant odour, containing C, H and O — that is ethanol, which
boils at exactly 78 °C.
**Boiling with concentrated H₂SO₄ gives a colourless gas.** At about 170 °C sulphuric acid
dehydrates ethanol:
C₂H₅OH ⇒ CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
**The gas decolourises bromine water and alkaline KMnO₄.** Both are tests for unsaturation,
and ethene passes both: it adds Br₂ across the double bond to give the colourless dibromide,
and Baeyer's reagent oxidises it to the glycol, losing the purple colour ✓
Check the alternatives: C₂H₅Cl (1) contains chlorine, not just C, H and O; C₂H₅COOCH₃ (2) is
an ester boiling well above 78 °C; C₂H₆ (4) is itself a gas, not a liquid.
∴ A is C₂H₅OH.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|36||0|0:
Benzaldehyde, C₆H₅CHO, has **no α-hydrogen** — the carbon next to its carbonyl is part of the
aromatic ring. With concentrated alkali it therefore cannot undergo an aldol condensation and
instead **disproportionates**:
2C₆H₅CHO + NaOH ⇒ C₆H₅CH₂OH + C₆H₅COONa
One molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidised to the salt of the acid, which is
exactly the pair of products named — benzyl alcohol and sodium benzoate ✓
This is **Cannizzaro's reaction**, and the absence of an α-hydrogen is its defining requirement;
methanal and formaldehyde behave the same way.
Perkin's reaction (1) condenses an aromatic aldehyde with an acid anhydride, Sandmeyer's (3)
replaces a diazonium group using a copper halide, and Claisen condensation (4) joins two
esters — none produces this pair.
∴ Cannizzaro's reaction.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|39||0|0.s:
A Grignard reagent, R–MgX, is strongly polarised R(δ−)–Mg(δ+), so the alkyl group behaves
as a carbanion. It attacks any carbon that is electron deficient — and that means any
polarised multiple bond to a more electronegative atom.
**>C=O** ✓ — the classic reaction, giving an alcohol after hydrolysis.
**–C≡N** ✓ — addition to a nitrile gives an imine salt, which hydrolyses to a **ketone**.
**>C=S** ✓ — a thiocarbonyl is polarised the same way and also adds the Grignard.
In every case the δ− carbon of the reagent attacks the δ+ carbon of the multiple bond, and
the electrons shift onto the electronegative atom.
Since all three are attacked, the answer must include them all.
(Grignards also add to CO₂, epoxides and acid chlorides for the same reason — and are
destroyed by any compound with an acidic hydrogen, which is why the apparatus must be dry.)
∴ all of the above.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|40||0|0:
The question turns on which metals are transition metals — those with partly filled d orbitals,
lying in the d block.
(1) Vitamin B₁₂ contains **cobalt**, Z = 27 — a transition metal.
(3) Haemoglobin contains **iron**, Z = 26 — a transition metal, and it is the Fe²⁺ that binds
oxygen.
(4) Insulin contains **zinc**, Z = 30 — in the d block, and usually counted here as a transition
element.
(2) Chlorophyll contains **magnesium**, Z = 12 — an s-block, alkaline earth metal with no d
electrons at all ✓
The Mg²⁺ sits at the centre of the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll and is essential to
photosynthesis.
It is worth noting the structural echo: chlorophyll and haem are built on the same porphyrin
framework, differing chiefly in whether Mg²⁺ or Fe²⁺ occupies the centre.
∴ chlorophyll.
kcet|Chemistry|2005|41||0|0:
Polymers divide by how their chains are connected.
**Thermoplastics** have long chains held to one another only by weak van der Waals forces or
hydrogen bonds. Heating lets the chains slide past each other, so the material softens and can
be remoulded repeatedly. Polythene, PVC and polystyrene are examples.
**Thermosetting plastics** are heavily **cross-linked**. During moulding, covalent bonds form
between the chains in all directions, so the whole specimen becomes a single giant
three-dimensional molecule ✓
Those cross-links cannot be broken by heating, so the plastic does not soften — it chars and
decomposes instead, and it can never be remoulded. Bakelite, melamine and urea–formaldehyde
resin are the standard examples.
This is also why thermosets are rigid and used for electrical switches and saucepan handles,
where softening would be dangerous.
∴ a thermosetting plastic.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|47||0|0.s:
A **nucleotide** has exactly three components:
1. a nitrogenous base
2. a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA)
3. a phosphate group
The nitrogenous bases are of two kinds:
**purines** — adenine and guanine, two fused rings
**pyrimidines** — cytosine, thymine (DNA) and uracil (RNA), one ring
So cytosine (1), guanine (2) and adenine (3) are all bases found in nucleotides ✓
**Tyrosine** is not a base at all — it is an **amino acid**, one of the twenty building blocks of
proteins. Its presence would indicate a protein, not a nucleic acid.
The similarity of the names is the trap: tyrosine against thymine and cytosine.
∴ tyrosine is not present in a nucleotide.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|50||0|0.s:
Two comparisons are needed: atom against its cation, and sodium against magnesium.
**Atom against cation** — removing electrons always shrinks a particle. The remaining
electrons feel the same nuclear charge spread among fewer of them, and for Na and Mg a
whole shell is lost:
Na (186 pm) ≫ Na⁺ (95 pm)
Mg (160 pm) ≫ Mg²⁺ (65 pm)
**Na against Mg** — both are in period 3, and magnesium has one more proton pulling its
electrons in, so Na is the larger atom and Na⁺ the larger ion.
Putting them in order:
Na (186) > Mg (160) > Na⁺ (95) > Mg²⁺ (65)
Mg²⁺ is the smallest of all, having lost two electrons to the greater nuclear charge — the
exact opposite of what is asked.
∴ Na is the largest.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|51||0|0:
Normality and molarity are related through the n-factor — the number of replaceable
hydrogens for an acid:
Normality = Molarity × n-factor
Sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, is **dibasic**: it can donate two protons, so n = 2.
Rearranging:
Molarity = Normality / n-factor
= 0.2 / 2
= 0.1 M
So a 0.2 N solution of sulphuric acid is only 0.1 molar — each mole supplies two equivalents.
The trap is option (2), 0.4, which comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
For a monobasic acid such as HCl the two measures coincide, which is why the distinction is
so easily forgotten; for tribasic H₃PO₄ the factor would be 3.
∴ 0.1 M.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|54||0|0.s:
Activated charcoal has an enormous internal surface area — the activation process opens up
a network of fine pores, giving several hundred square metres per gram.
Coloured impurities are generally large organic molecules. When the solution is passed over
the charcoal, these molecules stick to that huge surface by van der Waals forces and are held
there, while the smaller molecules of the substance being purified pass on.
This is **adsorption** — the impurity collects on the *surface* of the charcoal, it is not taken
into its bulk (which would be absorption) and it undergoes no chemical change.
That is the point of options (1) and (2): nothing is oxidised or reduced, so the purified
compound is recovered unaltered.
The same principle is used in gas masks, in water filters and in decolourising raw sugar.
∴ by adsorption.
